item.title: Building incus-hub: A Console for Multiple Clusters
item.description:
Yesterday’s conclusion was an open-source gap, and of the three roads I picked self-building — evolving the existing incus-hub (a multi-host aggregation page) into a multi-cluster console rather than starting over. This post lays out the design and the order of implementation, and closes the series with the one thing a no-replication architecture owes: backups as the only safety net.

Why evolve incus-hub

Everything v1 has gets reused:

Existing foundation How v2 uses it
Node with zero external dependencies (http/https/fs/path only) Runs directly on Debian 13’s stock Node 20.19.x; the systemd unit already exists
mTLS client certificates + per-host CA Becomes “one certificate per cluster + per-cluster CA”
callNode() / waitOperation() REST helpers Reused for handshake and operation polling
Promise.allSettled partial-failure isolation Upgraded to “a dead cluster greys out, the rest keep working”
Frontend aggregate table + search/filter + demo mode Gains the cluster hierarchy and a migration wizard

Not adapting Orcastra or LXD Mosaic, as covered last post: the former has no public source and wants 4 VMs / 30 GB of control plane; the latter flattens clusters into hosts, is PHP, and last shipped in 2022. None satisfy “light, runnable on Debian 13, controllable”.

item.title: P2P Production Best Practices
item.description:
Moving a P2P system from prototype to production involves engineering challenges across connection management, security, observability, and deployment. This article covers six critical areas with reusable code snippets and actionable guidance.

Connection Management and Resource Limits

P2P nodes must maintain a large number of simultaneous connections. Without resource caps, a node can suffer OOM crashes or file descriptor exhaustion. Production environments require strict control over three dimensions.

Three-Layer Resource Control Model
